content.introduction: The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates by another 0.25% when it releases its latest policy decision on Wednesday, bringing the benchmark interest rate range to 4.75%-5%, the highest since 2006. This decision comes amid a banking crisis and persistent inflation, creating a challenging position for the Fed. Fed Chair Jerome Powell will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET to explain the decision. While some sources suggest the Fed may hold rates steady this week, others indicate a potential hike in mid-December if inflation remains elevated. The decision is significant as it comes just seven weeks before the midterm elections, with Americans still dealing with high living costs.
body:
"They're in between a rock and a hard place," said Wilmer Stith, bond portfolio manager for Wilmington Trust. "There's a banking crisis and it's really a very tenuous, uncomfortable position for the Fed to be in."

During his semi-annual testimony before Congress in early March, Fed Chair Jerome Powell said strong economic data would likely push interest "higher than previously anticipated." [...] Forced to balance the consequences of a banking crisis and inflation that remains well above target, the Fed is expected to raise interest rates by another 0.25% when it releases its latest policy decision at 2:00 p.m. ET Wednesday afternoon. This move would bring the Fed's benchmark interest rate range to 4.75%-5%, the highest since 2006. Fed Chair Jerome Powell will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET to explain the Fed's decision. [...] Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell testifies before the House Committee on Financial Services on Capitol Hill on March 08, 2023 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) · Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images

"The Federal Reserve will definitely hike interest rates again, probably in December," Long said. "The big question is how many more times do they have to hike after that? And what was scary in this latest inflation data for September is to see so many areas of hot inflation: to see used car prices, airfares, recreation costs, auto repair costs, buying a used car, medical costs." [...] The market expects the Fed to hold rates steady this week, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 90.6% probability of rates remaining at their current target range of 3.75% to 4% – up from 84.5% a week ago and 35.8% last month.

For the Fed's meeting in mid-December, the tool shows a 75.1% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike, which could mark the resumption of the rate-hiking cycle if inflation remains elevated.
